p: Maria Santos had been a vice president for forty minutes when the letter arrived.

The office was on the fourth floor of the Cascade Valley Health administration building in Fort Collins, and it had a window, which was new. For fourteen years her office had been an ICU nurses' station in Greeley with a coffee maker that leaked and a view of a hallway. Then three years as nurse informatics director, in a cubicle. Then a year as Cascade's product owner on Penwright, the ambient documentation system that drafts the note while the clinician talks. That mostly meant a conference room at two in the morning. Then eight more months after go-live, keeping it boring. Now there was a window, a nameplate that still said the last person's name, and an inbox that already had two hundred and eleven messages in it.

Her new title was Vice President of Clinical Systems. It meant she owned the electronic health record, every clinical application that plugged into it, the interfaces that carried data between them, and the team of analysts who kept all of it running across eleven hospitals, forty clinics, and a home health agency. It meant she reported to Dr. Raymond Ochoa, the CIO, who had hired her by saying, You're the only person in this building who has been woken up by every system we own. I'd like that to stop being an accident.
The letter was a PDF attached to an email from a company most of Cascade had forgotten it paid.

An email from MedaLink Customer Success. Subject: End of support notice. Dear valued partner,. MedaLink will end support for the MedaLink EHR platform twenty months from the date of this notice. After that date we will no longer provide updates, security patches, regulatory changes, or help desk services. We encourage you to begin planning your transition now.

Maria read it twice. Eight of Cascade's hospitals ran Corvane, the system-wide EHR. Three didn't. Cheyenne, Laramie, and Rawlins had come in through an old affiliation with their own system, MedaLink, and everyone had agreed for six years that someone would deal with that eventually. She looked at the nameplate with the wrong name on it. She was apparently someone.
Her phone buzzed. A text from Lucia, seventeen, who was supposed to be in AP Chemistry. how's the big office. do u have a plant yet

Maria typed back that she didn't have a plant. Then she forwarded the letter to Ochoa with one line: I assume you've seen this. He replied in under a minute. I have. It's why you have that office. Breakfast tomorrow, 7:30, the diner. Bring a legal pad.
Ochoa's Legal Pad: the map of the territory.
Know what kind of place you're standing in.

Ochoa ordered eggs, pushed the plate aside, and drew a box on her legal pad. Before you fix anything, know what you own and who you serve. Healthcare isn't one kind of organization. An acute care hospital treats patients who need a bed and round the clock nursing. A critical access hospital is a small rural hospital, with no more than 25 inpatient beds, and special federal payment rules that keep care close to home in places like Rawlins. An academic medical center adds teaching and research. Ambulatory care covers clinics, surgery centers, and urgent care, where patients go home the same day. Community health centers serve patients regardless of their ability to pay. Home health brings nurses and therapists to the patient's house. Long term care and rehab handle the weeks and months after a hospital stay.

Then there are the organizations that never touch a patient but shape everything. Payers, like commercial insurers, Medicare, and Medicaid, decide what gets paid and how claims must look. Regulators, like CMS and state health departments, set the rules. Accreditors, like The Joint Commission, survey hospitals against standards. Public health agencies collect reportable diseases and immunizations. Research and academic institutions run studies and train the next generation. Every one of them wants data from Maria's systems, in a different format, on a different schedule.

How the exam asks it. HIMSS likes to describe an organization and ask what it is or what it needs. Match the services to the type: same day care is ambulatory, small rural inpatient care is often a critical access hospital, and an organization that pays claims is a payer.

Ochoa drew lines between the boxes. A patient in Rawlins sees a family doctor at a Cascade clinic, gets transferred to Cheyenne for surgery, goes home with a home health nurse, and has her claim paid by Medicaid. Every handoff is a place where information can get lost. Continuity of care is the idea that the next caregiver should know what the last one knew. A health information exchange, or HIE, moves clinical data between organizations that don't share a system, so the emergency department in Fort Collins can see the medication list from a clinic in Wyoming. Referrals, transfers, lab results, claims, and public health reports all travel across those lines.
When you change a system, Ochoa said, you change every line that touches it. People forget the lines.

How the exam asks it. When a question asks who is affected by a system change, the best answer usually reaches beyond the walls: referring clinics, the HIE, payers, public health, and the receiving hospital in a transfer.

The CIO owns the information technology strategy and budget for the organization and answers to the CEO and the board. The CMIO, a physician, bridges medicine and IT and leads clinical decision support and physician adoption. The CNIO does the same for nursing. The CISO owns information security: protecting systems and data from threats. The privacy officer owns how patient information is used and disclosed, and handles privacy complaints and breach assessments. A VP of clinical systems, like Maria, owns the clinical applications and the team that builds and supports them. Clinical analysts translate workflow into system build. Data stewards define and protect the quality of specific data. Superusers are front line staff trained to help their peers.

The lines matter. A clinical content decision, like what an order set should contain, belongs to clinicians through governance, usually a clinical informatics council. IT builds it. Security decisions belong to the CISO. Privacy questions go to the privacy officer. Your job, Ochoa said, isn't to make every decision. It's to make sure the right person makes it, on time, and writes it down.
How the exam asks it. Expect "who should" questions. Clinical content goes to clinicians and governance, security to the CISO, privacy to the privacy officer, overall IT strategy to the CIO.

Healthcare applications fall into families. Clinical systems support care: the EHR, computerized provider order entry (CPOE), the electronic medication administration record (eMAR), bar code medication administration (BCMA), the laboratory information system, pharmacy, and imaging through PACS. Administrative systems run the operation: registration and ADT (admit, discharge, transfer), scheduling, and supply chain. Financial systems handle the revenue cycle: charge capture, coding, billing, and claims. Consumer systems face the patient: the portal, telehealth, and remote monitoring. Business intelligence pulls data from all of them into a warehouse for reports, dashboards, and analytics. Lumen, the discharge forecasting tool Cascade licenses from Halcyon AI in Denver, lives there too: it reads ADT and census feeds and predicts who's likely to go home tomorrow.

MedaLink wasn't one system. In those three hospitals it was the clinical record, the registration system, part of the billing, and the feed to the HIE. Retiring it would touch every family on the list.

How the exam asks it. Know which family an application belongs to. Billing and claims are financial, registration and scheduling are administrative, the portal is consumer, and the data warehouse is business intelligence.

Ochoa turned the pad over. The board doesn't fund projects. It funds strategy. Strategic planning starts with the organization's mission, vision, and goals, then looks at the environment with tools like a SWOT analysis, then sets priorities. The IT strategic plan should trace back to the organization's plan, goal by goal. A project that can't show which goal it serves will lose every budget fight, no matter how urgent it feels to IT. Culture matters as much as the plan: the values, habits, and history of the people who'll live with the change. Three Wyoming hospitals that joined through an affiliation have their own culture, and they'll judge Maria by whether she learns it before she changes it.

How the exam asks it. When a question asks how to justify or prioritize an IT initiative, look for the answer that ties it to organizational goals. "Because the technology is better" or "because the vendor said so" is rarely the best answer.
Decision one. Whose call is it.

By ten o'clock Kiran Bhatt was at her door with a laptop and the look of a man who had been waiting for someone with authority. Kiran was the senior EHR analyst, a former pharmacy tech who built order sets the way some people build ship models.

Quick one. The Greeley hospitalists want the heparin order set changed. New starting dose, a different lab check. It's maybe two hours of build. You were a nurse, you know heparin. Can you just approve it so I can move it to production this week?
She did know heparin. She had given it a thousand times. What does Maria do?
A. Approve it now, since it's small, she knows the drug, and Kiran is waiting on it.
B. Ask Corvane's support line whether the change is safe, and follow what they say.
C. Tell Kiran to ask the Greeley hospitalists for written approval, then build it.
D. Send it to the clinical informatics council and build only what it approves.

Kiran sighs, but he files it. The council takes it up the next Wednesday. Pharmacy is at the table, catches the protocol mismatch, and the order set and the protocol change together. Dr. Aisha Rahman, the CMIO, who chairs the council with Maria, sends her a one line note: Thank you for not going around us.

That's the move. Clinical content belongs to clinicians, decided through governance. IT is the builder, not the owner. Routing it correctly is slower by a week and saves you from a patient safety problem. That's the trade every time.
Decision two. What MedaLink actually is.
Monday afternoon Maria opened a blank document and typed "MedaLink replacement." Then she stopped. She realized she didn't know exactly what MedaLink did.
She knew the nurses charted in it. She knew the doctors hated it. Beyond that, the three Wyoming hospitals were a gray box on every diagram she'd ever seen.
A. Treat it as an EHR swap and assume Corvane covers everything MedaLink did.
B. Get a replacement RFP out this month, since twenty months will go by fast.
C. Ask MedaLink for a full list of the modules Cascade licenses and plan from that.
D. Build an inventory of every function MedaLink does, who owns it, and its feeds.

It takes two weeks and a lot of phone calls. MedaLink turns out to be the clinical record, the registration and ADT system, part of the billing, the feed to the HIE, and the source for two state reports. Nobody had the whole list. Now Maria does.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. You can't replace what you can't describe. Inventory before you plan: every application, the family it belongs to, who owns it, and what it connects to. The gray box always has more in it than people think.
Decision three. Three hospitals, one plan.
Maria's first draft of a timeline treated Cheyenne, Laramie, and Rawlins as one unit. Same training plan, same staffing model, same go-live weekend.

Kiran read it and frowned. Rawlins has twenty-two beds. It's a critical access hospital. They have swing beds and an ER with one doc at night. Cheyenne is a regional referral center. I don't think they're the same project.
A. Do Cheyenne first as the pilot, then copy whatever worked at the smaller two.
B. Profile each hospital with its own leaders, then tailor the plan to each one.
C. Keep the single plan for simplicity, and adjust at Rawlins if problems show up.
D. Ask Kiran to rework it so each hospital gets its own training and staffing plan.

Maria spends an hour on the phone with each CNO. Rawlins needs training in four hour blocks over two weeks. Laramie has a surgical service that Cheyenne doesn't. Cheyenne takes transfers from both. The plan gets longer and a lot more real.

Exactly right. Know the type of organization before you plan for it. A critical access hospital and a referral center serve different patients with different resources. Tailor with their leaders, not around them.
Decision four. Who else is on the line.
Ochoa wanted a stakeholder list for One Chart by Friday. That was what he'd started calling it, One Chart, as if naming it made it real.
Maria's first pass had the three hospitals on it: their executives, nurses, physicians, and department heads. Forty names. It looked thorough.
A. Send it. The people inside the three hospitals are the ones who'll feel the change.
B. Map everyone the data touches: clinics, the HIE, payers, labs, and public health.
C. Ask each hospital CEO to name the stakeholders that matter for their site.
D. Add the vendors, Corvane and MedaLink, since they'll do most of the technical work.

The list grows to ninety names and fourteen outside organizations. Maria draws the lines on a whiteboard. Every line is a feed or a handoff that One Chart will have to keep working. Ochoa takes a picture of it with his phone.

That's the move. Interrelationships are the whole point. A system change at three hospitals ripples into referring clinics, home health, the HIE, payers, reference labs, and public health reporting. Map the lines before you cut any of them.
Decision five. Why we're doing this.
The next Tuesday, 7:30 AM, the first official one-on-one. Ochoa read her one page status and set it down.

Your page says we're replacing MedaLink because the vendor is ending support. That's true. It's also the weakest reason you could give the board. They'll ask why we don't just pay somebody to keep it limping along.
A. Tie One Chart to the system's strategic goals: one record, safety, rural access, and cost.
B. Emphasize the risk: unsupported software means no security patches after twenty months.
C. Ask Ochoa which reasons the board cares about and write those up for him.
D. Add a second reason to the page: Corvane is simply a much better product than MedaLink.

She pulls up Cascade's strategic plan. Goal one is a single patient record across the system. Goal two is safer transitions of care. Goal four is sustaining rural access in Wyoming. She rewrites the page so One Chart serves three of the five goals by name. Ochoa reads it twice and says, That one I can take upstairs.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Strategic alignment means showing which organizational goals the initiative serves. End of support is the trigger. The goals are the reason. Lead with the reason.
Kiran forwarded her a message from a Laramie nurse who'd seen the news on the intranet. He'd added only: FYI. This is the general mood.
A message from Laramie nurse, unit chat. so Fort Collins is coming to take MedaLink away. we built half of it. nobody asked us last time either
The three Wyoming hospitals had joined Cascade six years ago. Most of what they knew about Fort Collins came from memos.
A. Let it pass. People always grumble before a change and settle down later.
B. Ask the three CNOs to calm their staff down while she finishes the plan.
C. Post a reassuring message on the intranet explaining the benefits of Corvane.
D. Go to Wyoming in person, round on the units, and ask what they built.

She drives up Wednesday and spends two days on the floors in scrubs and a badge. A Laramie charge nurse shows her a MedaLink shortcut the staff built for transfer checklists. It's good. Maria writes it down and says so. By Thursday the unit chat has a new message: the new VP was a nurse. she actually charted with us.

Exactly right. Learn the organization's culture before you change it. These hospitals have their own history and their own values. Showing up, listening, and naming what they did well buys you the trust you'll spend for the next eighteen months.

Ochoa scheduled a virtual all-hands for the clinical systems team and the three Wyoming hospitals for the following Monday. Three hundred people, thirty minutes. It's your meeting, he said. I'll introduce you and then I'm furniture.
She had a plan that was two weeks old, a stakeholder map, and a lot of things she didn't know yet.
A. Walk through Corvane's best features with a demo so people get excited about it.
B. Wait to hold the all-hands until the full project plan and timeline are done.
C. Say what's happening and why, what's still unknown, and when they'll hear more.
D. Read the MedaLink notice aloud and explain that the vendor forced the decision.

She uses six slides. One says "What we don't know yet" in large type, with a date for each answer. She takes questions for fifteen minutes and writes every one on a list she posts that afternoon. The Laramie nurse from the unit chat asks a question. Maria answers it by name.

That's the move. Good business communication is clear, honest, and two way. Name the change and the reason, separate what's decided from what isn't, commit to when people will hear more, and give them a way to ask. Then keep the commitment.

Theo Reyes called Thursday. For ten years he'd been her night shift partner in the Greeley ICU, the one who showed up at 3 AM with two coffees and never asked if she wanted one. He'd left the bedside first, for informatics, and told her she'd be good at it. Now he was Director of Clinical Delivery at Penwright, and they'd spent a year of late nights getting Penwright live at all eleven hospitals. It had run clean for the eight months since.

Look at you with a window. Quick thing. The discharge instructions module is ready to build. Cheyenne asked for it first. We can integrate with MedaLink in about three months. Want me to put it on the schedule?
It would be a win for Cheyenne. And it was Theo asking.
A. Sequence it after One Chart, building it once on Corvane as part of the clinical portfolio.
B. Ask Cheyenne's leaders whether they'd rather have it now or wait until One Chart.
C. Ask Theo to build it as a standalone tool that doesn't connect to MedaLink at all.
D. Say yes. Cheyenne asked, Theo's team is ready, and it's a quick win for the hospital.

Theo doesn't argue. You sound like Irene, he says. Irene Kowalski had run nights in the Greeley ICU when they were both new, and she'd said build it once about everything from IV lines to schedules. For a second they're both back on nights. Build it once. I'll tell Cheyenne the why. Phase two goes on the roadmap for the month after go-live. One interface, one build, one set of testing.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Every new clinical application belongs in the portfolio, sequenced against what's already moving. Integrating with a system you're retiring doubles the cost and the risk. Build it once, on the platform you're keeping.
Decision nine. The ninety day plan.

Ochoa wanted her priorities for the next ninety days. Not just One Chart. Everything in clinical systems: forty open requests, two upgrades, the analyst team's backlog, and whatever was about to break.
Give me five things, not forty, he said.
A. Rank the forty requests by who's asking loudest and start from the top.
B. Do a quick SWOT with her leads, check it against the system's goals, and pick five.
C. Make One Chart the only priority and freeze every other request for ninety days.
D. Ask each analyst to send in their own top five, then combine all the lists.

She gets her leads in a room for two hours. Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, on a whiteboard. MedaLink's end of support is a threat. Marcus's interface knowledge is a strength and a weakness at the same time. Five priorities fall out, each tied to a system goal. Ochoa reads them and crosses nothing out.

Exactly right. Strategic planning starts with the mission and goals, looks at the environment with a tool like SWOT, and then sets a small number of priorities that serve the goals. Involving your leads gives you better information and their buy in.

Friday morning the head of cardiology at Fort Collins sent Maria a vendor brochure for a new heart failure app. Remote weight monitoring, a patient phone app, a dashboard for nurses. He'd already done a demo. We want it live by summer. Budget's not an issue, my service line has the money.
It looked good. It might even help patients.
A. Let cardiology run it as a pilot on their own, and evaluate it after summer.
B. Tell him no, because nothing new gets started until One Chart is finished.
C. Run it through intake against the strategic plan and what Cascade owns.
D. Approve it, since cardiology is paying and the app supports patient care.

Intake takes three weeks. The review finds Cascade already licenses a remote monitoring module in Corvane that does most of it. Cardiology pilots that instead, on Maria's analysts' time, and the heart failure program becomes part of the system's population health goal.

That's the move. Strategic alignment applies to every request, not just the big ones. Check it against the organization's goals, the existing portfolio, the architecture, and security. Often the answer is already sitting in a module you pay for.
Dr. Walt Hagen met her in the Laramie surgeons' lounge with a stack of paper. Thirty-one years in practice, reading glasses on a cord, a printed copy of every note he had signed that week.
I count clicks, he said. Forty-one to discharge a gallbladder in MedaLink. I'm told your new system is better. I've been told that three times in my career. Every time it was worse.
He wasn't hostile. He was tired, and he'd been right before.
A. Ask him to show her his discharge workflow, and invite him to help design it.
B. Ask the Laramie CMO to talk to him, since physician concerns belong to medical staff.
C. Promise him Corvane will take fewer clicks, since she's seen it at the other hospitals.
D. Explain that the decision is made, and focus him on how training will help him adjust.

He shows her all forty-one clicks, narrating. Three are a workaround for a lab feed that sometimes doesn't post. She writes that down twice. Then she asks if he'll sit on the physician design group. He looks at her over the glasses for a long time. Fine. But I'll tell you when it's worse. She says she's counting on it.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Respect the culture and the people in it. A thirty year surgeon's skepticism is earned, and his workflow knowledge is something you need. Listen, observe, and bring skeptics inside the design. They become your best testers.
Sunday night, Maria was asleep on the couch with a binder on her chest when her phone buzzed.
A message from Marcus Bell. lab results interface to laramie is down. relay queue backed up. looks like since about 8:30. nobody called it in. i can restart it but you should know.

Three hours. Relay was the interface engine that carried data between every system Cascade owned. Marcus Bell had built most of it, and nobody else really understood it. She had admin access to Relay; she'd been given it for the Penwright interfaces and nobody had taken it back. She could log in from the couch and restart it herself in five minutes.
A. Log in and restart the interface herself, then sort out the paperwork in the morning.
B. Tell Marcus to restart it, then go back to sleep and review it at Tuesday's meeting.
C. Have Marcus restart it under emergency change, and alert the Laramie supervisor.
D. Ask Marcus to wait until she reaches Ochoa and gets his approval to restart it.

Marcus opens an emergency change and restarts it at 11:52. Maria calls the Laramie house supervisor, who has the lab phone every critical result from the last three hours to the floors. A potassium of 6.8 reaches a nurse at 12:20. Then Maria opens a notes file titled "Why nobody noticed."

Exactly right. Roles matter most at midnight. The engineer fixes it through the emergency change process. Your job is patient safety and coordination: get clinical leadership running downtime procedures so critical results reach caregivers, and make sure someone owns finding the cause.

By 12:30 the queue was empty and the interface was green. Three hours of lab results had landed at Laramie all at once. Marcus typed queue's clear. Two words, which for Marcus at that hour counted as a conversation.
Lucia came downstairs at one for a glass of water and found her mother at the kitchen table in the blue light of a laptop. Is someone dying? she asked, the way teenagers ask things they half mean.
No, Maria said. Somebody almost didn't find out about a lab result. It's fine now.
Isn't that, like, the whole job? Finding out about the lab result? Lucia filled her glass and went back upstairs, leaving the question in the kitchen.

Maria thought about the week. Most of her calls had held up. Ochoa would still find the ones that hadn't. It had been a good first week. That was what bothered her. A good first week, and a lab interface had been dead for three hours without a single alarm.

She opened a new file and typed the question at the top. Not how it broke. Marcus would find that. The other question. Why had a lab interface to a hospital been down for three hours, in a health system with eleven hospitals and a twenty-four hour help desk, and nobody had noticed until one engineer happened to look?

At 6:45 AM her phone buzzed again. Ochoa. Heard about Laramie. I want to know why it took three hours before I want to know why it broke. And there's something else. The Joint Commission is at Greeley this morning. Unannounced.
